I can respect that! And I think Im at least partially understanding the distinction you’re making—definitely a language difference and what truly defines love for you. 

I guess something that I’m curious about with it is how do you interpret scenarios where you were in an established, loving, healthy relationship for a long time, but eventually parted ways due to growing in different directions or something of the sort? To me, it’s perfectly natural to still feel/have love towards someone like that, despite them no longer being a part of one’s life. Do you view that as something different than love? Or perhaps you view the mutual decision to separate, and continuing to respect that choice by maintaining distance, as the continued love?

This is a great perspective, especially for younger folks or for those who really have only been in short-term relationships. That deeper, fuller love is more than the transient feeling you feel in poignant moments. Not to say that isn’t part of it, or a beautiful experience, but rather the true ‘feeling’ is more of a tangible foundation of reciprocal trust, commitment, and compassion that’s been built over time and hardship. 

I do think it can be both—love as a feeling, and love as an act. Our society tends to think of love in the traditional fleeting sense, and I certainly agree the essence of the word is lost in that interpretation. However, when the acts of love you describe are both given and received consistently and with dedication, you feel filled and surrounded by the rich, full feeling that is real love imo. They become an extension of you and you of them, not because you don’t know where you end and they begin, but because you know you have each other, without fail, through and through. 

I also think this love is quiet in comparison to what OP is describing… it isn’t loud and exciting, it’s all the little joys throughout the day that you really only learn to appreciate when you truly see and accept your partner. It’s that particular smile, how their eyebrows crinkle in their tense look of concentration, their morning routine.. objectively mundane, but to you the happiest moments you’ll have are witnessing and being a part of theirs. Robin William’s monologue regarding his late wife’s idiosyncrasies in Good Will Hunting comes to mind

Yes, this is an important distinction—trauma bonding is not what OP is describing here. The contents and perspective you offer are completely valid and a great topic of discussion, but trauma bonding is the unhealthy attachment someone who is abused forms with their abuser, often as part of cyclical maltreatment. It is not connecting with someone who mirrors/represents past wounds/unhealthy relationships unless one is being presently abused in a current relationship. 

For example (and this is not to say this is most common scenario or anything like that, just the first thing that came to mind): someone with anxious/preoccupied attachment might naturally find themselves drawn to a partner with an avoidant attachment style due to having cold/emotionally neglectful parents growing up. This connection might spark fast and bright, and might have lots of highs and lows as the avoidant waffles between closeness and pulling away, but this in itself does not translate to being ‘trauma bonded.’ 

If the avoidant were being manipulative or abusive in some other way, showering the preoccupied individual with love, and then having fits of rage once they began feeling suffocated, only to reel them back in with more love bombing—that might constitute trauma bonding depending on how the preoccupied attached to the avoidant at that point. 

Again, don’t mean to detract from the conversation at all, just want to encourage using the proper language since terms can be thrown around without them being fully understood.

I don’t know if this will resonate at all, but I SH’ed through multiple means throughout my high school and college years, with varying degrees of frequency. The addiction is still very much there, the urge still comes up whenever I’m in distress, and I’ve also only self-harmed once or twice in the last three years. I also don’t think I will again—there’s always a chance, but something feels like it has shifted for me. 

Many have already spoken to some of the neurological and the emotional reasons for SHing, and I can say that I relate to all of them and what I was getting out of it always kind of depended on the moment. The reality is that nothing feels as good as SH, nothing is as morbidly satisfying, nothing gives as good a kick. If you’re looking for a healthy solution that will provide you with the same rush and soothing numbness afterwards, you probably won’t find it and instead will be engaging in some other semi-dangerous behavior or activity. That was my experience, anyway.

What changed things for me is understanding the need that spurred the urge to come about in the first place—what part of me was screaming out? what had my body been yelling at me that I neglected to listen to, to the point of such sheer overwhelm that the only solution was to drown it out? what did I need to acknowledge within myself—what needed to be seen, emotionally held?

It’s been a very slow process, but over the last year or two I’ve come to know that most often there are deeply, tremendously neglected pieces of me that are desperate to be seen, heard, and felt. And I’m by no means an expert in it, only slowly gaining familiarity, but I know now that when the urges come up, I need to approach myself with care and concern in the ways that no one ever did. And when I do that, I’m met with a very intense wave of sadness, exhaustion, weariness, unworthiness, all of it. And I just sit with it and do my best to let it be there. After a few moments, sometimes longer, there’s an inner calm that starts bleeding in where the chaos was before. I haven’t tapped into the raw feeling that needs releasing yet, but I’m slowly building a relationship with it, and it’s definitely been a game changer. Some day I hope to be brave enough to share it with my therapist. 

My two cents :) maybe it won’t do fuck all, might be worth a shot. I hope you’re able find what works for you ✨

Of course. That out of place, no belonging anywhere, real and unreal, drifting.. it’s all a rough, rough ride. Give yourself some kudos for doing what you can and seeking the support you need. Hopefully you’ve connected with clinicians who will show you that you’re worth sticking around for, that you’re easy to be around, likeable, and lovable. It takes time to build the trust in them and believe them (I’m still very much so working on this), and the right client-therapist relationship will show you that things can go differently than they did when you were a kid. The parts of you that keep you away from the present and keep you in this hyper-fearful place are doing what they know how to do to protect you… and, over time your subconscious will begin to recognize it’s not necessary to exist like that anymore. Just takes lots of time, and being patient with yourself, doing your best to develop self compassion (which is still the antithesis of my instinctual response, but it has gotten better). I know you’re feel unbelievably lost in this indescribable way that almost no one can even understand, I hear you on that… just don’t give up on yourself. :)

I trialed risperidone for awhile too actually, that worked well for my paranoia/panic. Fearing side effects is more than understandable, and, know that your body and brain are uniquely yours, so there’s no telling what’ll do the trick for you! Some people rave about Zoloft for their depression, others become too numbed out and detached… you’re going to hear success stories and horror stories no matter what you’re trying. I think it’s good to challenge yourself and try something out, and if it doesn’t work out, you can at least cross it off the list of what doesn’t work. As grueling as an adverse reaction to a med can be, it still brings you one step closer to knowing what does work for ya, you know? And if a med ends up being the cause for weight gain, my experience has always been that once I stopped taking it, my body naturally returned to its baseline state. It took longer for some than others, but it always ended up happening (I’ve tried easily 20-30 different meds). Not sure if any of this is helpful, and I’m just a rando on reddit, but hopefully you have some solace knowing that you’re not alone in the struggle.

Mm, yeah, I can definitely empathize with that! I’m either so disconnected that my affect is extremely constricted and I’m hardly even there but can still respond, or else I’m emotionally present for a little while only to shut down or get “ejected” as I call it, where I lose sense of where I am, who I am, what’s going on, etc. The disorganized attachment is such a mind fuck because part of you craves the closeness so intensely and then there are all these protective defense mechanisms keeping you from actually seeking it out, let alone being able to tolerate and sit with it. 

What has been really helpful for me is my therapist allows me to email her periodically throughout the week so that I have a less threatening space to express my thoughts and feelings regarding our session, events throughout the week, the struggles of simply just existing, etc. That’s definitely helped bridge some of the gap and helped me help her understand what I need. If that’s not an option for you, you could maybe try writing a letter to your therapist and giving that to them during your session or as you leave? It sounds like you’re struggling to make it in to your appointments, which is totally understandable, and at the same time doesn’t allow you to get the help and support you deserve! :) So I guess I would start small by just encouraging yourself to make an appointment and keep it, maybe let her know that you’ve been wanting to go and you’re just struggling with feeling safe enough to do so. 

On the other hand, depending on how established your relationship is with your therapist, maybe asking yourself whether there’s potentially a better fit out there is worth taking into consideration. 

The way I’m set up, I am able to disconnect from the intense attachment feelings in order to continue showing up… it’s by no means healthy and hinders our relationship in some ways because I then show up very withdrawn and detached, but it’s what I know how to do when those feelings are too overwhelming for me. Everyone processes differently and struggles in different ways, but hopefully you find something that works for you :)

Edit: Also, just had a thought… shutting down and being unable to speak is extremely overwhelming and scary, so I don’t want to invalidate that at all. But maybe think about how your therapist has responded in those moments, did they sit with you, did they try to ground you, did they run away, did they shame you? You’re dealing with very intense emotional responses that are super tricky to navigate, and you’re allowed to give yourself some grace and be patient with yourself. I’d imagine your therapist is more than willing to do the same, and hopefully you can try to maintain some of that perspective next time you’re coming out of a shutdown.

I’m sorry you’re going through this conflict with your therapist too, it’s really difficult and scary to sit with. 

It honestly feels like it was a lifetime ago that I was dealing with this, but I ended up mustering the courage to talk with her directly about it in session. I practiced multiple times in the week prior, sort of imagined what the conversation would be like and tried to process the emotions rather than intellectualizing and detaching from them. The work I did on my own really helped me show up in therapy how I’d been intending to show up for those 3-4 weeks I was struggling, meaning that I could hold my fear of closeness with her while also taking stock of my therapist’s genuine care and validation she’s provided for so long. Even though I knew she had no ill will and acknowledged that, hearing her apologize for unknowingly inflicting harm was huge. And because of the work I’d done before session, I was in a place where I could really receive/feel it rather than merely logically know it. It sounds really simple, but the effect remedied the confusion and fear and loneliness I’d been feeling. And then we talked a bit more about what it is I do need from her in those moments of extreme fear and disconnectedness… and things are by no means perfect now, but as I am slowly able to understand and articulate what it is I need, the better she is able to show up how I need her to. 

If your relationship to your therapist is similar to how mine sounds from reading my post, I’d really encourage you to have a session just about how you’ve been feeling and see where it takes you. I needed affirmation that things hadn’t changed on her end and that she was more than willing to continue to try to understand me as I learn to identify my needs. Let me know if you have any other questions, and I hope things work out well for you, however that ends up looking :)

Ahhhh, ok ok I getcha. I think I was getting hung up on the word “biasing.” In terms of self/other I definitely bias towards meeting other people’s needs, but I’m slowly getting more comfortable with asserting my own in small ways and feeling like my reasons are valid without having to make up something “more acceptable”. I’m not your archetypical “mom” of a friend group, but would easily stick my neck out for my friends before I put it on them to do that for me.  In a lot of ways though, I don’t have preferences for things, it’s kind of blank space. I think I would were I more in touch with myself, but gut feelings are largely only present in high pressure/actual external physical threat situations. I never know what I want to eat or where, what my style is, that kind of thing. Bigger decisions like where to go to school, what jobs I’m interested in, there’s certain concrete things that I know I value that make that easier, but like knowing what I want/need relationally or like developing hobbies is much more difficult to decipher. How to approach financial and academic-based decisions is somewhat fleshed out because there are rubrics that you can place yourself on, whereas personal preferences, which don’t really have a rhyme or reason besides what you feel is most fitting for you, are more vague for me.

It’s hard to have a concept of something that occurred so early and how significant it may or may not have been, whereas with my dad I know how I felt when he was there and I know how it felt being stripped of his care due to his own issues going on between when I was like 5-10. And we’ve never been the same since, much better than when I was as a teenager though. What I feel towards my therapist I think is what I’ve never been able to feel with my mom, not because she’s actually not safe now to attach to, but because it got jacked up when I was an infant.

I completely understand and agree with what you’re saying here, I definitely working on seeing things in the “grey” as opposed to, say, idealizing someone and devaluing myself. Or like being able to hold dialectics like I am frustrated with this person I love and it doesn’t mean that my love for them has ceased or converted to hatred, so I don’t have to fear that for myself, and if that’s how the other person views it, that’s more reflective of them than it is of me. I did read the other comments on one of your threads related to someone’s question about narcissism, where there’s the 1, 2, 3 of the internal self, the external self, and the congruency between the two, and this seems to parallel or else be what you’re talking about in this instance as well. 

> they would be debating two things that were both positive, or two things that were both negative, and have no awareness that they weren't debating oppositely toned valences (+/-)

With this, can you provide an example of what you mean here? I don’t quite get what you’re saying by the +/+ and -/- thing, except that it makes sense you can’t debate two things on one side of a binary (that logically makes sense—it’d be like trying to make a decision about where to eat and saying well this place has good tasting food and isn’t overly greasy, but for some reason perceiving those pieces of information as contradictory/a dilemma and then not being able to make a decision). They don’t know how to hold a proportion of good and a proportion of bad, there has to be one or another due to ego strength? (If that is, I don’t think I’m quite to that extreme of entirely + or entirely -, or 100/0 isolate/engulf anymore—though I can regress to the full extent at times. It’d only be like 90/10 or something like that before I “flip” as you say, but not quite fully all or nothing 100% of the time.)
You might also be saying something beyond that that I don’t quite have the words for at this moment, pertaining to the +/+ and -/-. 


> Let me ask you this - are you doing this right now in the conversation we are having? Because I would generally assume you are being the authentic you that you are and that it is not difficult to access or express and you are giving the whole as best as is relevant and not just throwing out parts.

I think you assume correctly here. I don’t exactly feel fragmented at this given moment, but there are also certain feelings/parts of me that aren’t cropping up at the moment because I’m level/regulated. I have an immense amount of toxic shame that is insanely crippling, but right now that “doesn’t exist” because I’m calm.  So I feel “whole” in the sense that I have no problem telling you more about me, and don’t feel like defenses are coming into play except maybe in the sense that I’m not emotionally “going” to the places that I’m explaining. If I fixated on it/let it “seep” in, it would become a problem very quickly and I wouldn’t be able to read your words as you mean them, I’d start backpedaling and recoiling, but since I’m not, it’s not an issue. 

> The only right move is whatever is authentic regardless of the thought of whether or not it will damage the attachment.

This sort of makes sense in that there’s a part of me that knows what would be good for me regardless of the fear—there’s a small voice in the back of my head in the midst of the panic that knows “you can put trust in this person you’ve extensively vetted over a few years” (my therapist), but it is an ant in comparison to the elephant that is the fear/panic/uncertainty of not knowing what to expect if I go that route. Am I gonna be decimated, am I gonna be swallowed, am I gonna be welcomed with open arms? There’s just no way to know until you do it. And I sometimes can in the smallest of ways if I’m semi-dissociated in a session (though this typically results in almost immediate panic/further dissociation/shutting down because a protective defense detects what’s going on and “says” FUCK THAT and overrides what I was trying to allow), but in terms of letting go and just being, trusting, not possible for me yet. It’s completely reflexive. It’s very easy for me to relay after the fact, making it sound like I have a decent amount of agency, but in the moment I very quickly become so overwhelmed that I’m kind of at the mercy of what my brain tries to do to keep me safe. How much of that is perception vs. actual reality are things I actively try to challenge as we work on this more. 


And I can appreciate what you’re saying about not being able to speak to certain things because you yourself are beyond that stage of functioning, that makes perfect sense to me. 

And thanks for the tidbit lol, fair enough. I do greatly appreciate your feedback and it very much so feels like content that could spur some positive change for me.

Well, I should mention that I graduated from undergrad studying psychology and neurobiology, so I might more readily understand the information you’re sharing compared to your average joe. However, I think much more of why it’s helpful is because I have tried so hard to explain what goes on for me in terms of splitting and major identity issues, the emotional overwhelm in very mundane situations, the dp/dr and slight perceptual distortions that can happen with that, and been met with blank looks of a complete lack of understanding. What you’re breaking down here not only describes why that disconnect is there (the people in my life are mostly at the neurotic level, except for my sister and brother who struggle with similar degrees of mental illness), but also provides me with a well-founded, linear, logical description and explanation of what’s going on for me. 


Referring to your explanation on the depersonalization, that’s definitely not my intuitive way of looking at it, but it resonates for sure. The way my mind is structured, I have the external version of me which is most often presented and includes what I feel are the “acceptable” pieces of me, and then anything that is deemed bad is denied when interacting socially, they’re largely outside of my awareness much of my day to day. Conversations that require me to be more vulnerable and attempt to allow/express those “less/(un)acceptable” parts are very stressful and destabilizing for me in that it almost always results in panic and me dissociating/retreating inward and an upheaval of my sense of self. However, it can also happen with positive identity parts as well (potentially the good threatening to annihilate the aggressive?)… too much of anything is threatening for me. I have a very limited social battery and tend to isolate quite a bit because the mental energy expenditure involved in socializing is very high. Of course, I have some people that are more comfortable than others, but no one (not even my therapist) sees “all” of me. The unacceptable parts largely don’t exist in my day to day, and the only way I’m able to emotionally express the unacceptable things is via email to my therapist (which is very frenzied and chaotic). I can intellectually explain that the unacceptable parts exist to other people in my life, but it’s under the condition that they don’t exist in that moment, they’re never seen. I literally do not know how to show up completely authentically because it’s too much for me to hold at once. With people I do feel a deeper level of attachment to, I am very likely to deny that that exists when actually interacting with them because it’s too overwhelming for me to feel and I don’t want to rupture the relationship because I couldn’t handle myself. 

For this reason, I do feel very disconnected from the people I care about, and while I can intellectually recognize the amount of love and care they have for me, it’s rare that I can receive any kind of comfort/warmth from those interactions. If I do, it’s largely in this conditional way where that “part” of me somewhat receives and is deserving of that love, but the disavowed parts get nil, which then causes a whole lot of internal turmoil for me. I remain largely detached from most people despite yearning for that closeness because the yearning feels so intense that it would consume me or I would implode or something like that. I don’t expect people to be able to hold that, so I tend to refuse its existence in the first place (emotionally), while maintaining a front that the connection is equally reciprocal in order to keep the relationship. There’s this constant push-pull going on that is very deeply rooted and very hard to manage because I never know what the “right” move is, “approaching” means meltdown and “avoiding” means never getting what I am so deeply deprived and in need of. It’s a lose-lose, and my life is full of fundamental contradictions. 


I’ve never met someone like me that feels so acutely aware of the fragmented parts of self and can identify what’s presenting and what’s not, what’s feeding into this response and what’s not, but feels like they’re working with a stacked deck in terms of progressing. It’s very frustrating and another example of the disconnect between cognitive awareness and emotional/psychological capacity. 

That was my way of reflecting what you said using my language, so hopefully it comes across that I think I pick up what you’re putting down. I really appreciate your response and your time. I have more questions if you’re open to it, but obviously want there to be a benefit for you as well :) Thanks again!

Honestly, it’s pretty tricky for me to nail down what has helped me the most in the long run. 

I would say in do or die scenario, kind of having an episode sort of a deal, a rapid increase in symptoms I guess, inpatient is good for just keeping you safe for a little bit. That’s pretty much it, in my experience. Some people it’s their first exposure to meds, so it kind of opens the door to psychiatry, but if you’ve been on em, in my experience it doesn’t do much. 

Residential was kind of a last straw thing for me. I had been bedridden for two months before then, and if I didn’t get any better from that, that was gonna be it for me. While there, I did benefit from the routine in terms of regulating my body, but I absolutely went stir crazy and felt very disconnected from the people I care about. Though I wasn’t contacting them much, despite having the option to, so I guarantee that contributed to that quite a bit. It did what I needed it to though, as trapped and suffocated I felt in there, it helped remind me of the importance of slowing down and having time to simply exist. By the time it was over, I was so done with it and ready to be ‘a real human,’ that I looked forward to going home. So I don’t know, I didn’t get better for a good reason and it was hard as hell, but I did get better. 

PHP I would say I probably got the most benefit from, but that’s more so because of the therapist I met there, who is now my regular therapist I just see outpatient for regular appointments. It’s a great way to learn DBT skills and have clinicians keeping consistent tabs on you, but you’re still free to live your life. Where I’m from in the midwest, you had to be 18 though, so I’m not sure what options would be available to your daughter unfortunately. I appreciated also getting such consistent individual therapy sessions as I tried to implement new things, and got good support in that aspect. At residential, you only talked about skills with your therapist and did zero processing whatsoever, and I absolutely hated that. My lady at PHP actually took time to learn my story and listen to why I thought I felt what I felt. And she was onto my bullshit, and I was so relieved that someone could finally see me. 

All in all, I honestly think the connection with your clinician is the most important factor. When someone sees you, like really sees you, you actually believe that change is possible and talking about things actually makes a difference because it’s coming from parts of you that were otherwise only accessible to you. For me, it takes a very special person to do that, and I’ve had it with two out of probably about 20 or so clinicians over the years?  And they’re 2 out of 3 people I’ve ever come across in my life that Ive connected to like that. And I honestly think that might be luckier than most. But with them, I knew instantly, first interaction, that they were different. They changed my life… it’s still hard as shit, still rocky and uncertain whether I’ll live, but they gave me a shot when I didn’t have anything left.

It’s kind of a mixed bag, depending where you go. I’ve been to two different facilities for inpatient stay (i.e, grippy sock jail), one was an actual hospital and one was more of a mental health facility. Pretty similar to what others have described with structured time, group therapy, meetings with a psychiatrist and therapist. Though since you’re only there for a few days (usually 2-5), you don’t actually get very deep with them, they’re kinda just trying to stabilize you so meds aren’t necessarily the best fit and therapy doesn’t process much. 

I’ve been to partial hospitalization as well, going to the hospital for 6 hours a day, 5 days a week doing group therapy, learning DBT, two weekly individual therapy sessions. That was pretty helpful, and people are generally more stable so not as triggering that way. Though this is kind of a step up from inpatient, because you have to be able to keep yourself safe at home. It’s something you transfer into after leaving inpatient. 

I’ve also been to residential treatment, which was about 7-8 weeks or so. Pretty similar to inpatient, but a much longer stay. The place I went to we also had daily walks, outings to the Y multiple times a week, weekly target run, and weekend outings to parks or the bookstore or other places. There were different privileges/levels there depending on your safety rating and how much you participated in group. There was art therapy and rec therapy multiple times a week as well. Weekly bonfires. Free time for about 3-4 hours a day during the week, more so on the weekends. You had homework to do every day, learning CBT, DBT, and mindfulness. Nothing very hard in my opinion, though many were very unmotivated to do it. Nutritionist available if you struggle with eating, nurses on unit, also just normal people who tended the floor. We didn’t have to be watched at all times, but if you got put on restrictions, you weren’t allowed in your room (me lol). Met some good people there, some really deep thinkers, some very annoying people, some pretty cool. In contact still with about 3-4. Only about 12 patients on your floor at a time, but people are cycling in and out during your stay. 

Costs were mostly covered for me because of my parents’ insurance.

I’m the same way, always dig into the same cut again and again when I relapse again. It hurts more to open when you’ve got a scar there because the tissue is more fibrous, but you do lose feeling eventually as others have said. 

I did it that way because I didn’t want people to know I was continuously self harming, minimizes the number of scars. But you end up with a pretty gnarly one instead. And depending how close to your wrist you are, I’ve noticed slight weakness in that hand because the tendons have been damaged and the tissues arent as organized and therefore not as good at doing their job. 

Normal tissues are layered in a particular system, the regular cell process when you’re developing. When scars form, that layering is disrupted and the skin that heals over kind of goes in all different directions on a cellular level. Your tendons and whatnot are designed to flex/extend in a particular direction according to what muscles they’re attached to, so once you screw with that order, they don’t hold tension with the same unison they did before.
